2611.13132.abstract: Altair (alpha Aql) is one of the nearest stars to the Sun at 5.13 pc and its age has recently been revised to 88+/-10 Myr, making it one of the youngest stars in the Solar neighborhood. This makes Altair a compelling target for high-contrast direct imaging searches for giant planets. We present two epochs of simultaneous F444W and F200W MASK430R JWST/NIRCam coronagraphic imaging observations. After post-processing, these data achieve F444W contrast levels of 2 x 10^-6 at 1" (5.1 au), 1.5 x 10^-7 at 2" (10.3 au), and a few x 10^-8 beyond 4"(20 au). Using the Sonora Flame Skimmer models, this corresponds to sub-Jupiter mass sensitivity beyond 5 au and sub-Saturn mass sensitivity beyond 10 au. We identified several candidate point sources in the field in the first epoch data. Second epoch observations confirmed that none of the candidates were co-moving with Altair and their colors are consistent with background stars. Altair has no known companions, no detected debris disk, and is not associated with any stellar association. Despite this, its youth and proximity ensure it will remain a high-priority target for future high-contrast imaging observations. We additionally discuss Altair as a potential reference star for future observations, presenting measurements of background sources in the field and showing that Altair will remain at least a few arcsec from background stars over the next 10-20 years, making it a reliable reference target for upcoming imaging campaigns including the Roman Space Telescope Coronagraph Instrument.

2611.13257.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic comparison of standard starlight subtraction (top) and our method based on physical modeling, FLIP (bottom). The stellar PSF is shaped by inevitable and imperfectly-known aberrations in the telescope (including star-coronagraph misalignment and optical phase aberrations, represented by colored curves to the left of the diagram). Starlight subtraction methods based on empirical reference images are limited by telescope instabilities that cause changes in these aberrations, since these result in dissimilar reference PSFs (symbolized with curves and image outlines of different colors) and thus imperfect PSF subtraction when combining them into an empirical PSF model. Our method FLIP pre-calibrates an instrument model on reference images to reproduce the reference PSF, and then solves for small changes in telescope aberrations that better explain the science image. This is represented by the optimization loop that tunes aberration estimates with arbitrary flexibility (and thus closer to the effective aberrations that produce the science PSF, represented by the red curves), beyond the limited aberration diversity provided by imperfect reference PSFs in standard approaches. This circumvents the stability limit of the instrument and enables imaging of fainter planets.

Figure 2: Stellar PSF subtraction comparison between our method FLIP and standard method KLIP. Top: Observations re-processed in this work with KLIP, using the same algorithm hyper-parameters as in their respective publications. In all cases our re-processed KLIP results are comparable with the published results 31; 26; 32. Middle: Data processed with FLIP, showing the full field of view optimized over (80$\times$80 pixels). Bottom: Our detected companions with FLIP next to ideal simulated PSFs, to highlight the recovered morphology and to distinguish real point sources from PSF side lobes. The SNR of the detection is shown in the upper right corner of each panel. Accounting for small sample statistics following 3, the confidence of the detections from top left to bottom right correspond to 23.7$\sigma$, 5.7$\sigma$, non-detection, non-detection, 26.3$\sigma$, 8.8$\sigma$, 5.3$\sigma$ and 7.7$\sigma$. The position of the star is marked with a star-shaped icon. In all panels, North is up and East is left. 51 Eridani F430M observations are convolved with a Gaussian kernel ($\sigma=$ 1 px) to smooth out pixel-to-pixel noise (only in this panel is pixel-to-pixel noise comparable with the brightness of the companion).

Our method enables significant improvements (in some cases $4-15\times$) in exoplanet detection sensitivity. 2611.13257.abstract: Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation. Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation. Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories. Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff) to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2-15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b at 4.3 $\mu$m. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.

2611.13321.title: The climate and potential habitability of a warm and oxygenated Mars

figures.caption: Figure 1: Simulated habitability of a warmed Mars as a function of atmospheric pressure (x-axis) and grey gas forcing (symbol colour). Each symbol’s position on the y-axis corresponds to the global average temperature for one of our simulations. Black contour lines correspond to the fraction of the surface with temperatures and oxygen levels allowing some life to grow; blue contour corresponds to the threshold where, at some places on Mars, humans can live without a pressure suit. Increasingly green shading shows pressure–temperature conditions that permit photosynthesis but not humans. Increasingly red shading corresponds to lifeless climates.

Figure 2: As Mars’ surface temperature increases with pressure and grey gas forcing, diurnal temperature variations (top panel), defined as the difference between the temperature at 3 pm and the temperature at 3 am local time, decrease due to warmer nights. Seasonal variations (bottom panel) increase with grey gas forcing but decrease with pressure due to greater heat transfer by advection.

Figure 3: Zonal average surface temperatures at four seasons (from left to right: Northern spring equinox, Northern summer solstice, Southern spring equinox, Southern summer solstice), as a function of datum pressure and grey gas forcing. Day and night temperatures
correspond to local times of 3 pm and 3 am respectively. Rising atmospheric pressure warms nighttime temperatures at all latitudes, but cools daytime temperatures
over latitudes where the Sun is directly overhead.

Figure 4: Increasing the pressure (left to right panels) and grey gas forcing (top to bottom panels) warms nighttime air temperatures (blue) in Hellas (latitude 42.5° S, longitude 69° E, 6.8 km below datum) near the surface, reducing the day–night temperature range. However, seasonal variations are only slightly reduced. Even at high
atmospheric pressures, high grey gas forcing can cause daytime
highs above the boiling point of water. When the atmospheric
pressure is 5 times that of present-day Mars, Hellas is at the threshold (Armstrong limit) below which humans would require pressurised suits to prevent blood boiling. Each column header shows the pressure at Mars datum ($P_{dat}$) and that within Hellas ($P_{Hel}$). We plot seasonal variation as a function of solar longitude $L_{s}$ ($L_{s}=90$ is Northern summer solstice, $L_{s}=270$ is Southern summer solstice).

Figure 5: Temperature, pressure and oxygen limits on growth of organisms for simulated climates on Mars as a function of atmospheric pressure (left to right) and grey gas forcing (top to bottom). Water-availability and soil-chemistry constraints on life are ignored, so the extents shown are upper limits. At low pressure, the low boiling point of water and low oxygen partial pressure only allow for simple, hardy organisms to grow. As the atmosphere builds up, more complex organisms can be established in the relatively temperate equatorial lowlands. In the legend, organisms are listed from most to least resistant to atmospheric stressors (reading down from the top to the bottom of the first column and then again from the top to the bottom of the second column), as described in A and Tables S1-S2. Where two or more organisms overlap, we show the constraints for the least resistant one. We distinguish human survival without pressure suits but with oxygen masks (‘with oxygen’) from human survival when breathing Mars air (‘unaided’).

Figure 6: As the pressure increases, the boiling point of water rises, allowing for a greater temperature interval with surface liquid water. In turn, this widens the surface area that has seasonal surface temperatures within the range of liquid water (middle panel), allowing for more opportunities for life to grow on the surface. When the atmospheric pressure is $\geq$15 times that of present-day Mars, small regions of Mars have surface temperatures that permit year-round surface liquid water (bottom panel).

Figure 7: Estimated net production rate of oxygen over the area that would sustain organisms (Fig. 5) if the production rate is assumed to be 33 mol/m2/yr for plants and lichens (equivalent to tussock grass, Shaver and Chapin III 1991) and 26 mol/m2/yr for cyanobacteria (equivalent to 50% of industrial production rates, Verseux et al. 2016). Dashed lines correspond to the assumption that the productivity of regions in which only mosses and lichens can grow is 0.8 mol/m2/yr, equivalent to the lower productivity end of tundra environments on Earth (Whittaker, 1975). Cyanobacteria are assumed to only grow poleward of 45° latitude, where data suggest near-surface ice. The local dip in the productivity when $kP_{dat}=0$ and $P_{dat}=91.5$ hPa is due to the spatial resolution of the model; at these pressures, only a few pixels poleward of 45° permit cyanobacteria.

2611.13321.abstract: We present the first 3-D Global Climate Model simulations of an oxygen-rich, terraformed Mars. Assuming an O2-CO2 atmosphere, with additional warming from a well-mixed grey gas, we study (1) how surface temperatures change with atmospheric pressure and grey gas opacity, and (2) how temperature, pressure, and other effects limit life as oxygen builds up. We neglect the climate effects of dust and the water cycle, as well as possible soil-chemistry and nutrient limits to life. We find that (1) increasing grey gas opacity and increasing atmospheric pressure both moderate day-night temperature swings, but only slightly reduce seasonal temperature swings. Climate remains harsher in the Southern mid-latitudes relative to the Northern hemisphere. (2) For an atmospheric pressure of 30 hPa (5 times its present-day value), temperatures on Mars would be consistent with lichen and moss, followed at 60 hPa by forests (initially in the Hellas Basin). However, creating a human-breathable atmosphere through photosynthesis alone, at the oxygen production rates of biomes on Earth today, would take at least thousands of years, and require more oxygen than can be made via photosynthesis of known CO2 reserves on Mars alone (unless CO2 is recycled).

2611.13343.abstract: Planetary transits require a fortuitous alignment between a planet's orbit and our line of sight, but dynamical interactions can render this geometric coincidence only temporary. We report the discovery of the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, the first confirmed planet orbiting a single star whose transits have been directly observed to disappear. Over seven years of photometry from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), the planet's transit chord traversed and eventually moved off the stellar disk entirely, with an impact parameter changing at the rate of $\dot{b} = 0.16\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The transit mid-times also show significant departures of $\pm 6$ hours from a linear ephemeris. Joint modeling of the transit timing and duration variations (TTVs and TDVs) and NEID radial-velocity data indicates the presence of a nearby, mutually inclined ($i_\mathrm{mut} \gtrsim 5^\circ$) planetary perturber, with the TDV being primarily due to precession of the planets' orbital planes. Our dynamical modeling reveals that the perturber is likely of Saturn-mass or greater and in a mean-motion resonance with TOI-2535 b, making this an unusual system that contains two short-period giant planets. The TDVs measured for TOI-2535 b represent one of the most extreme examples of planet-planet interactions driving orbital evolution on human timescales.

2611.13505.abstract: Transit timing variations are a powerful method for detecting non-transiting planets, particularly in systems near mean-motion resonances. We investigate the ultra-short-period hot Jupiter TOI-2109 b using 87 transit epochs spanning two decades (2006-2025), combining observations from TESS, CHEOPS, HST, and ground-based photometry. We compare five timing models representing different physical scenarios: a linear ephemeris, orbital decay, apsidal precession, a sinusoidal model, and a two-planet n-body dynamical model. The orbital-decay fit yields $\dot{P} = -3.96 \pm 2.05$ ms yr$^{-1}$, providing no significant evidence for ongoing orbital decay. The sinusoidal model reveals a periodic transit-timing-variation signal with an amplitude of $\approx 44\,s$. Dynamical modelling favours an additional non-transiting companion near the 7:3 mean-motion resonance with an orbital period of $1.57813\pm 8.9\times10^{-5}$ days and a mass of $0.70 \pm 0.02\,M_{\rm Jup}$. The two-planet model yields $\Delta \mathrm{BIC}=4.95$ relative to the sinusoidal model, indicating positive evidence that the observed transit timing variations are best explained by gravitational perturbations from an additional planet.

2611.13771.title: Breaking the Chain: The Dynamical History of the Barnard's Star Planetary System

figures.caption: 图 1: Distribution of adjacent-planet period ratios in confirmed multi-planet systems. The data were retrieved from the NASA Exoplanet Archive on June 3, 2026.
图 2: Adjacent planet triplets in Barnard’s Star system and their closest three-body resonances. The observed period ratios have negligible errors at levels of $10^{-4}$.
图 3: Scenario IA: Tidal expansion of an initially resonant four-planet chain toward the observed period ratios.
图 4: Scenario IB: Magnetospheric rebound of an initially resonant four-planet chain toward the observed period ratios.
图 5: Scenario IIA: Tidal expansion disrupts the initial five-planet resonance chain by breaking the adjacent 3BRs. A subsequent merger of c1 and c2 yields the present-day period ratios.

图 6: Scenario IIB: Lindblad torques expand the inner resonant chain during the disk phase. The resonance between planet c2 and e breaks first, followed by instability in the system and a planet merger. The disk dissipates once the planets approach the observed period ratios.

图 7: Evolution of the period ratios in one example simulation of Scenario IA ($i=45^{\circ}$, $Q_{\mathrm{phy}}=20$). Left panel: period ratios of planets d, b, and c; right panel: period ratios of b, c, and e. The red dashed lines represent three-body resonances ($(p,q,r)=(2,3,5)$ for d–b–c and $(5,4,9)$ for b–c–e). Other dashed lines show other close three-body resonances. The planets expand along the resonant lines until $\sim 8$ Gyr, after which the resonance breaks.

图 8: Evolution of the three-body resonance angles for the same simulation as Fig 7. The 3BR angles for the adjacent triplets (d, b, c) and (b, c, e) are shown, together with the non‑adjacent combinations (d, b, e) and (d, c, e). The adjacent (d, b, c) and non‑adjacent 3BRs librate and drive the resonant expansion until $\sim 8$ Gyr.

图 9: Evolution of the normalized $B$-value (Eq. 3) for the same simulation as Fig. 7 for the adjacent triplets (d, b, c) and (b, c, e). The shaded bands indicate the $1\sigma$ observed ranges from Table 1. The libration amplitude never reaches the observed offset, even before the resonance breaks.
图 10: Evolution of the semi-major axes (solid lines), pericenter and apocenter (dashed lines) in the closest-matching Scenario IB simulation. The dash-dotted line marks the disk inner edge.

2611.13771.abstract: Barnard's Star is the nearest single-star system to the Sun and hosts four recently detected sub-Earth-mass planets. The system exhibits architectural imprints of a "broken resonant chain". We explore scenarios in which the presence of a now-lost, additional planet provides a more natural explanation for the present-day architecture from a dynamical-formation perspective. In such a situation, a resonance-breaking event triggered a merger between two planets, forming the present-day planet c. We find two viable pathways that can reproduce the observed configuration: (i) stellar-driven, long-term tidal expansion and (ii) disk-driven, early expansion, in which one-sided Lindblad torques separate the two outermost planets. Both scenarios can lead to the c1-c2 merger required to form the present-day architecture. The latter pathway also agrees with the broader exoplanet census: among the 14 compact four-planet systems we identify with broken-chain architectures similar to Barnard's Star system, ten have the third planet "breaking" the resonant sequence.

2611.14330.abstract: I search the single-epoch detections of the NOIRLab Source Catalog DR2 (DECam, 2012-2019) for outer Solar System objects. Single-night detections are linked with a bound orbit model, vetted against artefacts, static sources and known objects, and confirmed by forced measurements on at least two new archival nights. The linker recovers 96% of known objects present on four nights in one sky tile, but end-to-end recall is about 7%, limited by cadence, tiling and catalogue incompleteness; no selection function is provided. Of 81 catalogue objects, four are designated; of the other 77, 53 are in evidence class A (multi-opposition, at least nine nights), 12 in class B and 12 in class C (not counted). On exposures never used in a fit, forced photometry detects 41 testable objects at 99% of predicted positions, as for known TNOs, against 6% at control positions; 22 pass a post hoc rule, 19 are inconclusive, none fails. Shifted controls were never confirmed by the archival image search (0 of 11,467) but were in 2.2% of trials by the catalogue precovery behind most scripted confirmations, so its nights alone are not sufficient. For the 65 class A and B candidates, 10-Myr integrations give four candidate L4 Neptune Trojans with 13-19 yr arcs, 21 resonant, 13 detached, nine scattering, two Centaurs and 16 classical objects; a detached class-B candidate has q=48.8 au. No object beyond 80 au was confirmed, which barely constrains Planet Nine. Positions are withheld until designation or 2027 June 30; their digests are published.

2611.14441.title: Nucleation of water ice under weak ionization via clustering on negative ions

figures.caption: Figure 1: Free electrons collide with water molecules to produce positive and negative ions, predominantly $\mathrm{OH^{-}}$ and $\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}$; water molecules cluster around the ions; positive clusters are neutralized by the electrons, while negative clusters grow into stable ice grains. Cottin [10] shows that the electron energy for producing $\mathrm{OH^{-}}$ is about 4.5 eV whereas the electron energy for producing $\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}$ is about 12 eV.

Figure 2: (A) Schematic of the experiment. (B) Image of laser light scattered off ice grains (green) suspended within the plasma (purple) at 130 K; individual grains are visible, and are enlarged in the overlay at left. (C) Image of scattered laser light at 170 K; the grains are much smaller and scatter the light diffusely.

Figure 3: Mass spectra of positive clusters (A) and negative clusters (B), collected at 245 K, and smoothed with a 6-amu gaussian window to show long-range behavior. (C) and (D) show the variation of mass spectra with temperature, from 210 to 250 K. Concentrations of clusters about bare $\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}$ (E) and $\mathrm{OH^{-}}$ (F) with sizes $n=1$ to 4, relative to concentration of the bare ion, are plotted as temperature is steadily decreased.

Figure 4: Comparison between classical theory, DFT simulations, and experimental results. A: the Gibbs free energy predicted by Eq.(1) using $P_{H_{2}O,\infty}=4$ Pa, $P_{sat}(T)$ given by [34], $p=6.19\times 10^{-30}$ C-m, $\gamma=0.109/(1+2\delta/r)$ N/m with $\delta=-0.4$ $\mathring{A}$, $r_{i}=1.1$ $\mathring{A}$, $\varepsilon_{r}\gg 1$. B: The Gibbs free energies, computed from DFT, for several clusters. For clarity, only odd-numbered clusters are plotted, and only the lowest-energy configuration for each cluster size. C: The stable cluster size satisfying $d\Delta G/dn=0$ from Eq. 1 (black), the average cluster size measured in experiment (red), and the average cluster size predicted by DFT (blue). Error bars on experiment and DFT sizes indicate the spread of the cluster size distribution. D: timescales associated with positive and negative ion neutralization, ambipolar diffusion of positive ions, and ion hydration, and the 1 ms on/off time of the RF power modulation. The 3-body hydration rates for $n=0-2$ are taken from [16].

Figure 5: A: Gibbs free energy for nucleation about an OH- ion (Eq. 1) at protoplanetary disk parameters corresponding to $R=20$ AU and $Z/R=0.2$, using values from Agúndez et al. [1], where the H density is $10^{9}$ cm-3 and the relative water abundance is $10^{-9}$. At this location, Agúndez et al. [1] indicates $T=70$ K, at which the plot is monotonically decreasing, and so ice will spontaneously nucleate on an OH- ion. B: Same as panel A, except for noctilucent cloud parameters at 85 km, where air pressure is 0.35 Pa and water vapor is 2 parts per million, as given by Gumbel and Megner [19]

2611.14441.abstract: Water-ice grains are shown to form spontaneously in a cold, weakly-ionized laboratory plasma with trace water admixture when neutrals and ions are cooled below $\sim$200 K. These conditions serve as an analog of ice nucleation in cold astrophysical and atmospheric environments. The ice grains form without the presence of particulate impurities, and do not form in the absence of ionization, indicating that nucleation is induced by ions. Time-resolved ion mass spectrometry provides separate detection of clusters of water molecules on both positive and negative ions. Hydrated negative ions, mainly $\mathrm{OH^-(H_2O)_n}$, grow to $\sim$200 amu, while hydrated positive ions, mainly $\mathrm{H^+(H_2O)_n}$, remain small and short-lived. As the temperature is reduced from room temperature toward 200 K, negative ion clusters grow in size and then drop sharply in abundance, consistent with the onset of rapid growth into macroscopic ice grains below a critical temperature. This indicates that hydrated negative ions are key precursors to ice nucleation in cold, weakly ionized environments, such as the Earth's mesosphere and protoplanetary disks, providing a concrete pathway for ice formation in environments where the nucleation mechanism has remained unresolved. This negative ion pathway is estimated to dominate over ice deposition on pre-existing dust grains in protoplanetary disk locations where there is sufficient UV to partially dissociate water molecules, and in addition, where negative ions such as OH- can form readily through electron attachment at low temperature.

2611.12910.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Predict Atomic Oxygen Erosion of Polymers in Low Earth Orbit

figures.caption: Figure 1: Workflow for polymer erosion yield ($E_{y}$) prediction. Space mission data are first collected across four spacecraft orientations: Ram, Nadir, Zenith, and Wake. The data is then preprocessed and formatted for training, followed by the fine-tuning of a GPT base model using prompt–response pairs. The resulting fine-tuned model is subsequently used to predict the $E_{y}$ for new polymer systems.

Figure 2: Erosion yield dataset overview. (a) Frequency of each polymer’s assigned chemistry/PSMILES string in the dataset. For readability, each PSMILES string is referred to by its corresponding “polymer name”. (b) Distribution of fluence values. (c) Distribution of erosion yield ($E_{y}$). The blue, red, yellow, and green colors depict the Ram, Wake, Zenith, and Nadir sample orientations, respectively.

Figure 3: Fine-tuning workflow for erosion yield ($E_{y}$) prediction. The curated dataset, containing PSMILES, experimental conditions and log-transformed $E_{y}$ values, is divided into different splits. Prompt–response pairs are constructed with structured system and user prompts, and then used to fine-tune a base LLM. The resulting fine-tuned model is employed for inference to predict the $E_{y}$ of unseen polymer chemistries.

Figure 4: 
Effect of training epochs and inference temperature on GPT-4o performance. (a,b) Parity plots comparing predicted and experimental erosion yield ($E_{y}$) values after fine-tuning for 5 and 10 epochs, respectively, across five held-out test sets. The dashed line denotes perfect agreement ($y=x$). Each panel reports the corresponding order-of-magnitude error (OME) and log-R2. (c,d) Dependence of log-R2 and OME, respectively, on the temperature used during inference.

Figure 5: Effect of macroscopic features on model performance. Parity plots comparing predicted and true erosion yield ($E_{y}$) values for models trained (a) without thickness and number of layers, (b) with number of layers and (c) with thickness as a feature, across five train-test splits.

Figure 6: Workflow for evaluating the fine-tuned GPT-4o model and benchmarking it against Gaussian process regression (GPR). The dataset is partitioned using random and restricted-group train–test splits to assess interpolation across known chemistries and generalization to unseen polymer chemistries, respectively. Both models were trained on the same experimental measurements but differed in how the polymer and associated descriptors were represented and encoded.

Figure 7: A comparison of model performance across data splitting strategies and informatics methods. Parity plots of predicted versus true erosion yield ($E_{y}$) are shown for fine-tuned GPT-4o using (a) the restricted-group split, containing only Ram-oriented measurements of unseen chemistries, and (b) the random split, including all four orientations, and for GPR using (c) the restricted-group split and (d) the random split. Data points are colored by AO fluence, illustrating model performance across different exposure conditions and highlighting the relationship between AO fluence, sample orientation, and erosion yield. The final GPT-4o models were fine-tuned with optimized hyperparameters.

2611.12910.abstract: Low Earth orbit (LEO), home to most active satellites, is projected to undergo a debris-fragmentation cascade known as Kessler Syndrome. In light of this eventuality, it is imperative to maximize the operational lifetime of LEO satellites. Instrumental to this goal is the development of next-generation polymeric materials with improved resistance to atomic oxygen (AO) erosion. Because genuine LEO exposure experiments are prohibitively expensive and LEO conditions are difficult to reproduce in the laboratory, data-driven approaches offer a promising alternative for accelerating materials discovery. Here, we develop a fine-tuned large language model (LLM) based on OpenAI's GPT-4o to predict the AO erosion yield ($E_y$) of polymers using a curated dataset of 201 measurements compiled from multiple NASA LEO exposure missions. The model achieves an order of magnitude error (OME) of 0.154 and a log-scaled coefficient of determination (log-$R^2$) of 0.719, outperforming conventional machine learning approaches while eliminating the need for extensive feature engineering. Notably, incorporating macroscopic descriptors such as film thickness and layering did not improve predictive performance, suggesting that AO erosion is governed primarily by chemical and environmental variables rather than bulk structural characteristics. This finding underscores the importance of chemically informed polymer design in developing materials with improved AO resistance, while demonstrating the ability of modern LLMs to effectively extract chemically meaningful relationships even when data is limited. Beyond its predictive accuracy, the proposed framework provides a scalable platform for rapidly screening candidate polymers, reducing reliance on costly spaceflight experiments.

2611.13064.title: Mars Seed: A Reference Architecture for Biomanufacturing Habitats from Martian Resources
2611.13064.abstract: Human exploration of Mars will require enormous quantities of materials for the first crewed missions and substantially more for permanent habitation, making flexible and scalable technologies for in situ resource utilization (ISRU), including biological ISRU, of significant interest. However, no existing mission architecture quantitatively evaluates whether in situ biomanufacturing can realistically deliver materials at the scales required for human settlement. Here, we present Mars Seed, an end-to-end reference architecture for using biomanufacturing to produce bioplastics at scale entirely from in situ resources on Mars. We provide a complete analysis of a space bioprocess in which feedstocks are generated entirely from Martian resources, converted biologically into polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) bioplastic, and purified to produce material suitable for constructing human habitats. We show that the upfront power and upmass costs of deploying the equipment required for this bioprocess are recovered within two synodic periods relative to Earth-shipped alternatives. Further, because the process relies entirely on feedstocks sourced from Martian materials, production can continue until equipment failure without requiring additional materials from Earth, enabling scalable conversion of local resources into useful materials. Mars Seed demonstrates that biological ISRU can be mass- and power-competitive with Earth-shipped alternatives, establishing biomanufacturing as a practical component of Mars mission architecture rather than an aspirational capability.

2611.13128.title: Planetary material is a major source of hydrogen in helium-atmosphere white dwarfs

figures.caption: Figure 1: Evolutionary phases and pathways of He-atm WDs considered in our model. Distinct phases are represented by cells A–J, whose labels and colours indicate their spectral features. Stars in the first row have never accreted planetary material (‘pristine’), and their primordial hydrogen may or may not be detectable (cells B and A, respectively). If and when they accrete planetary material, they move downwards along the pathways shown as green arrows, and cannot return to the top row. The middle row corresponds to He-atm WDs that have detectable atmospheric pollution. For He-atm WDs with no primordial hydrogen, the accreted material may be hydrogen-poor or hydrogen-rich (C and D cells, respectively). The third row contains He-atm WDs that have accreted planetary material, but whose metals have sunk out of their photospheres and are thus untraceable. Cell side lengths are labelled with the parameters of our model, as described in the main text. While the arrows show potential evolutionary pathways, it is critical to understand that our model is applied to a population snapshot, where the number of stars in a given phase at the moment of observation is static.
Figure 2: The minimum $$f$$raction f of He+H WDs that have accreted planetary hydrogen. Probability density distributions for f based on each dataset are generated by bootstrapping.

Figure 3: Distributions o$f$ model $$p$$$$a$$rameters (p, a, $$h$$) and the minimum fraction (f) of He+H-atm WDs that have accreted planetary hydrogen from the bootstrapping analysis, where p is the fraction of He-atm WDs whose primordial hydrogen is detectable, a is the fraction of He-atm WDs that have ever accreted planetary material (’accretors’), and h is the fraction of accretors lacking in primordial hydrogen that have detectable planetary hydrogen, in the conservative limit where the fraction of accretors with detectable metals is set to $d=1$. Contours represent the 1-, 2- and 3-$\sigma$ regions of the distributions. NB this figure does not represent a formal posterior probability distribution, but rather shows the range of solutions that are compatible with the bootstrapped data. Fig. 2 is a zoom into the lower-right panel of this plot.
Figure 4: Distributions of values compatible with the bootstrappe$d$ data when d is free to vary, following Fig. 3.

Figure 5: Veri$$f$$ication that results do not strongly depend on the choice of S/N cut. Top panels: S/N and Gaia G magnitudes of candidate He-atm WDs for inclusion in the samples, with the presence of metals (Z) or hydrogen indicated as in the legend. Shaded regions indicate our S/N cuts, corresponding to the lowest-S/N He+H+Z-atm WD in each catalogue. The two tracks in the DESI plot reflect e$x$posure time differences between dark- and bright-time observing programs. Bottom panels: Solid lines and shading show the minimum value of f and its 1-$\sigma$ uncertainty calculated after applying a cut on S/N $\geq x$ at each point on the x-axis, i.e. excluding all stars to the left of that point. The minimum value of f calculated from our final samples are shown as dashed lines, with 1-$\sigma$ uncertainties as dotted lines.

Figure 6: Veri$f$ication that results do not strongly depend on the choice of colour cut. Top panels: Hertzsprung–Russell diagram showing candidate He-atm WDs for inclusion in the samples. Symbols and shading have the same meaning as in Fig. 5. Dotted lines show cooling tracks for pure He-atmosphere white dwarfs (Bédard et al., 2020) with masses in the range 0.4–1.0 $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$, with temperatures indicated by vertical marks. Bottom panels: minimum value of f and its 1-$\sigma$ uncertainty calculated after applying a cut on $G_{\mathrm{BP}}-G_{\mathrm{RP}}\geq $x$$ at each point on the x-axis, following Fig. 5.

Figure 7: The relationship between colour and S/N in the DESI sample, showing that a more stringent S/N cut than we made would bias the sample against redder (cooler, older) objects, changing its character.

Figure 8: The Ca ii K line from simulated white dwarf spectra with the resolution and wavelength spacing of DESI across a range of effective temperatures. The other stellar parameters are fixed to $\log{g}=8.0$, $\log{\textrm{H}/\textrm{He}}=-5.0$ and $\log{\textrm{Ca}/\textrm{He}}=-8.0$, representing a moderate level of metal-enrichment.

2611.13128.abstract: Many white dwarfs with helium-dominated atmospheres show traces of hydrogen in their spectra. On average, the total mass of hydrogen within their convective envelopes increases with age, but there is no consensus on the origin of such hydrogen. Hypotheses include upward diffusion from hidden reservoirs deep within the envelope, or accretion, alongside heavier elements, of planetary material. We construct a simple model that includes both pathways, and test it using two independent samples of helium-atmosphere DB white dwarfs from the DESI and SDSS spectroscopic surveys, selected to have Gaia colours BP-RP > -0.25, corresponding roughly to 10000 < $T_{\rm eff}$ < 19000K. We find that at least $22 \pm 2$ per cent of the helium-atmosphere white dwarfs with detectable hydrogen must have accreted some of it from their planetary systems, via ices, hydrated minerals or atmospheres. We thus demonstrate that planetary hydrogen is a necessary ingredient to explain the spectral evolution of white dwarfs as a population, rather than only extreme hydrogen-enriched cases.

2611.13136.title: Near-Ultraviolet and Optical Observations of the White Dwarf ZTF J0328$-$1219 Reveal Variable Periodicity in its Transiting Debris System

figures.caption: Fi$$g$$u$r$e 1: 2024 November 2-5 ULTRACAM g-band (black) and $g{-}r$ (gray) light curves phase folded on $P_{\rm A}=9.937$ hr (left) and the conditional entropy periodogram of combined, averaged g & r light curve (right). A prominent transit centered around Phase$\,\approx\,$0.38 persists across the four consecutive nights. We annotate on the periodogram $P_{\rm A}$ and $P_{\rm B}$ as red and light blue triangles, respectively. Only the A period is significant to the nominal $10\,\rho$ threshold (see Section III.1), delineated by the dash-dotted green line. The disappearance of features in the flat $g{-}r$ light curve indicates achromatic transits (Section IV.1).

Fi$g$u$r$e 2: 2025 October and November light curves of ZTF J0328$-$1219 phase-folded on $P_{\rm B}=11.17$ hr, the best measured period for this epoch (Section III). Light curves are color-coded by bandpass (BG40: black, g & $V$: green, r: red, NUV: light blue, and unfiltered: white) and each observatory is assigned a unique marker shape. Repeating patterns are detectable early on, such as at Phase $\approx$ 0.5 during Cycles 1, 4, and 6. The transit morphologies evolve much more rapidly at later cycles and no longer show obvious repeating patterns at this period. This dynamical activity is corroborated by the changing periodograms in the bottom panel of Figure 3. The offset between Cycles 16 and 17 is boosted to account for the enhanced total flux excursion observed by HST and LAST. Some light curves are binned by a factor of two or three for improved visibility.

Figure 3: Lomb-Scargle (top) and conditional entropy (middle and bottom) periodograms of our 2025 autumn optical light curves of ZTF J0328$-$1219. The top and middle panels incorporate the entire dataset, while the bottom panel is partitioned into three windows of $4-7$ nights. Each panel shares the same frequency axes. Multiple harmonics of $P_{\rm B}$ (red triangles) and $P_{\rm A}$ (light blue triangles) are significant beyond the bootstrapped 0.1% false-alarm probability and 10 $\rho$ thresholds for the Lomb-Scargle and conditional entropy periodograms, respectively, each delineated as dash-dotted green lines. In the top panel we inset the spectral window to clarify our resolution. We inset in the middle panel our Gaussian fit to the core of $P_{\rm B}$. The bottom panel highlights rapid variations in the periodicity of the transits, where over the course of the campaign the light curves shift from being dominated by $P_{\rm B}$ to $P_{\rm A}$. A new period emerges during the final window, $P_{\rm C}$ (yellow triangle). Aliases are likely present, namely 7/5$\,f_{\rm A}$. The rapidly varying periodicity suggests ongoing dynamical activity within the system that is bringing material from the various orbits into and out of view, matching the morphological complexity within the light curves of Figure 2.

Figure 4: Comparison between the transit depths as seen in the NUV with HST/STIS to the optical as observed by LAST (binned from 30-s to 60-s exposures to match the effective HST sampling). We calculate the transit color term in the right panel using only data separated by no more than 60 s. We use orthogonal distance regression to measure the reddening law $E(\mathrm{\textsc{nuv}}-\mathrm{\textsc{optical}})/A_{\mathrm{\textsc{optical}}}=0.59\pm 0.08$. The residual variance of the best-fit line (4.06; solid gold line) is preferred to the null hypothesis, the fixed horizontal line (5.84; dashed gray line). This color term is intrinsic to the data during fifth HST orbit; we measure $E(\mathrm{\textsc{nuv}}-\mathrm{\textsc{optical}})/A_{\mathrm{\textsc{optical}}}=-0.10\pm 0.12$ considering only the second through fourth HST orbits. The particle size distribution could significantly vary dip-to-dip and over consecutive orbital cycles as collisions rearrange the transiting debris, however, the fifth orbit data are the most normalization-dominated and their transits the shallowest. Over HST orbits 2-4, NUV starlight is constantly preferentially extincted given by the best-fit y-axis intercept of the linear fit being $A_{\mathrm{\textsc{nuv}}}=A_{\mathrm{\textsc{optical}}}+0.18\,$mag.

Fig$u$re 5: Model spectrum of ZTF J0328$-$1219 (red) superimposed over our HST/STIS spectrum in the NUV (top, gray) and optical SOAR/Goodman spectrum (middle, gray). We highlight several prominent metal transitions seen as absorption and the Lyman $\alpha$ wing in the NUV, along with insetting a magnification of the optical Ca-II H and K transitions. Our SOAR spectrum exhibits absorption at the sodium D doublet ($\lambda\approx 5900\,$Å) with no detectable absorption at H$\alpha$. The bottom panel compares the SED photometry to the model from the NUV to the NIR. Red circles correspond to the model fluxes and the photometry is shown as the black error bars without markers. The silver error bars represent the SDSS u and GALEX nuv photometry and are only shown for reference.

Figure 6: Photospheric abundance ratios of select elements with respect to calcium derived from our model spectrum of ZTF J0328$-$1219, all normalized to the Solar metallicity (gray dashed line). We consider build-up (charcoal squares), steady state (blue circles), and declining phase (orange triangles) accretion scenarios. The debris is consistent to within 1 $\sigma$ with a composition akin to CI chondrites (yellow dashed-dotted line) and delivered via build-up accretion, except for silicon. Our carbon detection is about 2 dex enriched relative to the expectation for bulk Earth material (green dashed-dotted line).

Figure B.1: Light curves folded on $P_{\rm A}=9.937\,$hr. It appears possible that Cycles 14 and 16 and Cycles 19 and 22 show evidence for being influenced by transits from this orbit. All light curves are plotted in the same fashion as that of Figure 2.

Figure B.2: RVO and HAO light curves from 2025 October 29-November 3, the same grouping of light curves used for the third window in the bottom panel of Figure 3, folded on $P_{\rm C}=7.64\,$hr. A transit recurs through Cycles 0-9 at phase$\,\approx 0.6$, despite conditional entropy indicating 7.69 hr is the best period. Our RVO light curves during the nights of November 2 and 3 lacked the phase coverage to resolve the transit further.

Figure B.3: Our entire collection of 2025 October-November follow-up light curves (top) and the maximum total flux excursions computed over 1-hr bins of each light curve (bottom). Our HST observations notably occurred during the point of greatest activity we sampled. All light curves are plotted in the same fashion as that of Figure 2.

Fi$$g$$$u$$r$e C.1: ULTRACAM $ugr$ light curves from 2024 November (top panels) and associated color term distributions. Despite the apparently significant color terms from u vs. g and g vs. r, the residual variances of the linear ODR fits (salmon-colored lines) are indistinguishable from the null hypothesis of a horizontal line (i.e., colorless transits). See Section IV.1.

2611.13136.abstract: We observed the transiting debris disk system around the white dwarf ZTF J0328$-$1219 using the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) in 2025 October, obtaining near-ultraviolet (NUV) spectroscopy with STIS over five consecutive HST orbits. Our abundance analysis supports the accretion of a chondritic body. We complemented our HST program with 16 days of optical time-series photometry beginning in 2025 October, which reveal variable periodicity and rapidly evolving transit morphology. Previous monitoring by TESS during Sectors 4 and 31 confirmed a predominant, stable transit orbital period, $P_{\rm A} = 9.937$ hr, along with a second, transient period, $P_{\rm B} = 11.2$ hr. Our 2025 autumn light curves show transits are dominated by $P_{\rm B} = 11.17$ hr with $P_{\rm A}$ initially appearing as a weaker, secondary feature and eventually returning to predominance. We also identify a candidate transit period of 7.64 hr during the final days of the 2025 autumn campaign, although its significance and persistence remain uncertain. We add simultaneous $ugr$ light curves collected with ULTRACAM in 2024 November that are dominated by $P_{\rm A}$ and show no significant color term. We further compare the transit depths in optical photometry concurrent with our NUV observations, again measuring a lack of transit-dependent extinction except during the fifth HST orbit where a reddening term may arise. The observed variable periodicity and potentially changing color behavior illuminate ongoing dynamical processes, namely collisions, and demonstrate the opportunity for studying dust physics in real time at white dwarf debris disks.

2611.13260.abstract: Atmospheric variability provides a unique window into the three-dimensional structure, dynamics, and evolution of brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres. Recent JWST time-resolved spectroscopic observations have revealed complex wavelength-dependent variability, offering unprecedented insights into cloud structures, thermal perturbations, and atmospheric chemistry. However, existing programs have focused primarily on individual benchmarks and specific scientific questions, resulting in heterogeneous spectral and temporal coverage and leaving important regions of the substellar population underexplored, particularly across a broad range of rotation periods, spectral types, and viewing geometries. A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program could systematically investigate substellar weather across a diverse, well-characterized population. By combining broad infrared spectroscopic coverage with observations spanning multiple rotations and strategically selected epochs, this program would constrain the contributions of different physical mechanisms while investigating how atmospheric structures depend on rotation, viewing geometry, and fundamental physical properties. Extended monitoring would also improve rotational-period determinations and reveal how atmospheric features evolve from rotation to rotation and over longer timescales. This coordinated effort would provide a consistently designed and uniformly processed dataset of time-resolved spectra and variability diagnostics, enabling population-level comparisons, testing predictions from three-dimensional circulation models, and establishing a framework for interpreting the atmospheric diversity and evolution of brown dwarfs and directly imaged giant exoplanets.

2611.13770.abstract: Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4) provides epoch astrometry from which thousands of giant planets and many substellar and stellar companions can be characterised. We present ExoPlanetLab, an open-source package for Bayesian orbit inference from Gaia epoch astrometry, radial velocities (RVs) and relative astrometry, validated on simulated and real data. The model orbit is compared with the epoch residuals after removing the part absorbed by the single-star fit. A Student-t likelihood describes heavy-tailed data. A robust Keplerian periodogram with bootstrap false-alarm probabilities gives starting values for a joint fit. Five samplers are available: tempered ensemble MCMC, two nested samplers and two reversible-jump samplers. Evidences for a fixed number of companions select that number. Acceleration and scan-angle models test whether an orbit is warranted. The samplers agree within 0.1 sigma on a simulated two-planet system. In 180 injections all fits converge, and all signals with signal-to-noise ratio S >= 10 are detected. The posteriors show no significant bias, but the period coverage is below nominal: 90% of the true periods lie within their 95% credible intervals. None of 30 companion-free data sets gives a false detection. On DR4 pre-release data the orbit of Gaia BH3 is recovered within 1.4 sigma of published solutions. The Student-t model brings the astrometric period and eccentricity of HD 114762 onto its RV orbit. Eight simulated relative positions narrow the period's credible interval to 0.27 of its width, and Octofitter agrees within 0.2 sigma on the same data. The code is validated for single sources with DR4-like epoch astrometry, with or without RVs. Relative astrometry is tested on simulated data only. The main limits are an uncorrelated noise model and the computing cost, which grows linearly with the number of measurements and steeply with the number of companions.

2611.14151.abstract: The exchange in specific orbital energy between a test particle in a Keplerian binary orbit and a continuously incident linearized gravitational wave (GW) is considered. Analytical expressions for the rate of change of energy, semi-major axis and mean motion of the test particle are derived. Numerical solutions illustrate a resonance effect betwen the GWs frequency and the particle's initial orbital frequency. We distinguish between bounded short-period oscillations and resonant libration. The effect of the GWs angle of incidence with the particle's orbital plane is also considered. Using an illustrative high GW strain we show that changes to the eccentricity are bounded while inclination exhibits small linear growth for an initially flat, circular orbit. Long coherence requirements linit the observational significance of GW resonance to astrophysical systems with very short orbital periods.
